Max-Cut and community detection" subtitle: "AIDAMS -- S7" author: "Guillaume Lecué" institute: | ![](Logo-essec.jpg){width=200px} engine: knitr format: revealjs: theme: serif slide-number: c/t width: 1600 height: 900 margin: 0.08 scrollable: true transition: fade auto-stretch: false css: custom.css knitr: opts_chunk: dev: "svg" fig.ext: "svg" engine.opts: template: "tikz-template.tex" dvisvgm.opts: - "-n" - "--libgs=/opt/homebrew/lib/libgs.dylib" --- # Matrix lifting and SDP relaxation [An introduction example: finding a top eigenvector]{.subtitle style="font-size: 1.3em;"} ## Exercises :::{.box-yellow} **Exercise 1:** Let $x\in\bR^n$. 1. What are the size and the entries of the matrix $Z=xx^\top$? 2. How can you write $\norm{x}_2^2$ using $Z$? 3. How can you write $\norm{Ax}_2^2$ using $Z$ where $A$ is a matrix? ::: . . . :::{.box-yellow} **Exercise 2:** Show that $Z$ is positive semidefinite, rank 1 matrix if and only if there exists $x\in\bR^n$ such that $Z=xx^\top$. ::: . . . :::{.box-yellow} **Exercise 3:** Let $f, g:x\mapsto x^\top M_fx, x^\top M_gx$ be two quadratic functions. Let $K = \{x:g(x)\leq1\}$. Write the problem $\min_{x\in K} f(x)$ with variable $x$ into a problem with variable $Z=xx^\top$. What are the pros and cons of this transformation? ::: ## The lifting device :::{.box-green} **Idea:** Any (purely) quadratic problem in $x$ (i.e. a quadratic objective and quadratic constraints without linear terms) can be rewritten as a linear problem in $Z=xx^\top$. ::: . . . :::{.box-yellow} **Exercise 1:** Let $x\in\bR^n$. What are the size and the entries of the matrix $Z= \begin{pmatrix}1\\x\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\end{pmatrix}$? **Exercise 2:** Write any quadratic problem in $x$ (that may contain linear terms) into a problem with variable $Z= \begin{pmatrix}1\\x\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\end{pmatrix}$. ::: . . . :::{.box-red} **Lifting device**: transform a 'vector' quadratic problem into a 'matrix' linear problem. The **price** to pay is that we go from dimension $n$ to dimension $(n+1)^2$. ::: ## Problem: find a leading eigenvector {.smaller} :::{.callout-tip title="Problem statement" icon=false} Let $A\in\bR^{n\times n}$. Find $x\in\bR^n$ such that $\norm{x}_2=1$ and $\norm{Ax}_2$ is maximized. ::: **Classical solution:** The most efficient way to solve this problem is to use the [power method]{.red}: take $x_0\in\bR^n$ at random and iterate $x_{k+1} = \frac{Ax_k}{\norm{Ax_k}_2}$. . . . **An alternative solution is using the lifting device:** $$ (P_x) \quad \max_{\norm{x}_2=1}\norm{Ax}_2 = \max_{\substack{Z\succeq 0\\ {\rm rank}(Z)=1\\ {\rm Tr}(Z)=1}}\inr{A^\top A,Z} \quad (P_Z) $$ Because: $\norm{Ax}_2^2=\inr{A^\top A,xx^\top}$, $\norm{x}_2=1$ iff ${\rm Tr}(xx^\top)=1$ and $Z=xx^\top$ iff $Z\succeq 0$ and ${\rm rank}(Z)=1$. Moreover: $v_1$ is a leading eigenvector of $A$ (i.e. a solution of $(P_x)$) iff $Z=v_1v_1^\top$ is a solution of $(P_Z)$. . . . ::: {style="height: 40px;"} ::: :::{.box-red} **Problem:** The rank $1$ constraint is not convex. **Solution:** Drop the rank constraint! ::: ## SDP relaxation for the problem of finding a leading eigenvector Dropping the rank constraint, we get the following optimization problem: $$ \max_{\substack{Z\succeq 0\\ {\rm Tr}(Z)=1}}\inr{A^\top A,Z} \quad (P^\prime_Z) $$ **Questions:** - What kind of optimization problem is $(P^\prime_Z)$? - What do we lose by dropping the rank constraint? . . . ::: {.box-red} - We get an SDP problem: this is what we call an **SDP relaxation**. - We lose nothing! This relaxation is **exact**: $(P_Z)$ and $(P^\prime_Z)$ have the same optimal value and the same optimal solution(s). (this is not always the case!) ::: ## Take away message from this introduction example: :::{.box-blue} We have seen **matrix lifting**: transforming a vector quadratic problem in $x$ into a matrix linear problem in $Z= \begin{pmatrix}1\\x\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\end{pmatrix}$. The price to pay is that we go from dimension $n$ to dimension $(n+1)^2$. ::: :::{.box-blue} We have seen **SDP relaxation**: dropping the rank constraint in a matrix problem to get an SDP problem. Sometimes, this relaxation is exact, but sometimes it is not. ::: . . . Next, we will see how to use these techniques to solve two problems: - The Max-Cut problem, - The community detection problem. # Matrix lifting and SDP relaxation [Example 2: the Max-Cut problem]{.subtitle style="font-size: 1.3em;"} ## What is a graph? ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (graph)" icon=false style="font-size: 0.9em;"} A **graph** is a pair $(V,E)$: $V$ is the set of **nodes**, and $E\subset V\times V$ is the set of **edges**. A **weighted graph** is a triple $(V,E,W)$ with $W\in\R^{|V|\times|V|}$. The entries of $W$ are the **weights**. ::: :::{.spaced-list-two} - **Undirected graph:** $(i,j)\in E$ implies $(j,i)\in E$. - **Undirected weighted graph:** the graph is undirected and $W=W^\top$. - Four classical types of graphs: directed or not, weighted or not. ::: ## Four types of graphs ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Undirected/directed and unweighted/weighted graphs.](matrix_lifting_SDP_relaxation_files/figure-revealjs/graph-types-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ## Complete graphs and a ring graph :::: {.columns style="display: flex; align-items: center;"} ::: {.column width="62%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Complete graphs $K_4$, $K_5$ and $K_6$.](matrix_lifting_SDP_relaxation_files/figure-revealjs/complete-graphs-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="38%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A directed ring graph.](matrix_lifting_SDP_relaxation_files/figure-revealjs/ring-graph-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=85%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Adjacency matrix ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (adjacency matrix)" icon=false style="font-size: 0.9em;"} Let $G=(V,E)$. The **adjacency matrix** $A\in\{0,1\}^{|V|\times|V|}$ is $$A_{ij}=1\quad\text{if }(i,j)\in E,\qquad A_{ij}=0\quad\text{otherwise.}$$ For a weighted graph, $A_{ij}=W_{ij}$ when $(i,j)\in E$ and $A_{ij}=0$ otherwise. ::: - If $G$ is undirected, then $A$ is **symmetric**. - The Max-Cut and community detection problems are about the **connectivity** of $G$, which is encoded in $A$. - Everything is inside $A$ (all graphs problems are matrix problems): **Adjacency matrix** is the central mathematical object in graph theory. ## Exercise: International Trade Network {.smaller} **Question:** The bipartite graph below represents annual exports (in billions of €) between France (FR), the UK, and Germany (DE). Construct the $3 \times 3$ adjacency matrix $A$ for this directed, weighted graph. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![International Trade Network.](matrix_lifting_SDP_relaxation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=70%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fragment} **Solution:** Assuming the node order is **1: FR**, **2: UK**, **3: DE**: $$ A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 30 & 70 \\ 25 & 0 & 40 \\ 65 & 50 & 0 \end{pmatrix} $$
*Note: $A_{i,j}$ represents the edge from node $i$ to node $j$. For example, $A_{1,2} = 30$ means FR exports 30 to the UK.* ::: ::: :::: ## The Max-Cut problem ::: {.box-blue style="font-size: 0.7em;"} Given an undirected and unweighted graph $G=(V,E)$, a **cut** is a partition $S\sqcup S^c=V$ of the nodes. The **Max-Cut problem** is to find a cut that maximizes the number of edges across the cut. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](matrix_lifting_SDP_relaxation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=40%} ::: ::: **Example in Frequency Allocation:** Nodes are cellular towers, and edges represent overlapping broadcast radii (interference zones) (possibly weighted by the population density in that overlap). Finding the Max-Cut assigns the towers to Frequency 1 (set $S$) and Frequency 2 (set $S^c$) such that the maximum amount of interference is neutralized. ## Exercise: Finding the Max-Cut **Question:** Consider the graph $G=(V,E)$ below. Find a partition $S \sqcup S^c = V$ that solves the Max-Cut problem. What is the value of the maximum cut? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](matrix_lifting_SDP_relaxation_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=60%} ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="60%" .fragment} **Solution:** The Max-Cut value is **4**. **The Partition:** $S = \{1, 3\}$ and $S^c = \{2, 4\}$. **Why?** Because nodes 1, 2, and 3 form a triangle, it is impossible to cut all 5 edges (any cut of a triangle can cross at most 2 of its 3 edges). Therefore, the theoretical maximum is $5 - 1 = 4$. By grouping the diagonal's endpoints (1 and 3) into the same set $S$, we make $(1,3)$ the only internal edge. The cut edges are: $(1,2), (2,3), (3,4),$ and $(4,1)$. ::: :::: ## Formulation of the Max-Cut problem :::{.box-yellow} **Exercise:** Write the mathematical formulation of the Max-cut problem. ::: . . . ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: MAX-CUT maximizes over all possible cuts the number of edges across the cut: $$\max_{S\subset V}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}\mathbf{1}_{i\in S,\,j\in S^c}$$ where $\mathbf{1}_{i\in S,\,j\in S^c}$ is the indicator function of the event $\{i\in S,\,j\in S^c\}$: $$ \mathbf{1}_{i\in S,\,j\in S^c} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i\in S \text{ and } j\in S^c \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ ## Equivalent formulation of the Max-Cut problem :::{.box-yellow} **Exercise 1:** Show that the Max-Cut problem is equivalent to $$\max_{S\subset V}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}\mathbf{1}_{i\in S,\,j\in S^c}=\max_{x\in\{\pm 1\}^n}\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}(1-x_ix_j).$$ **Exercise 2:** Show that one can find a solution to the Max-Cut problem from a solution to the following problem: $$\min\big(x^\top Ax:x_i^2=1\big) \quad (\dagger)$$ ::: . . . ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: :::{.box-blue style="font-size: 0.9em;"} - Is $(\dagger)$ an easy problem to solve? - What sort of problem is $(\dagger)$? - Can you suggest a convex surrogate problem for $(\dagger)$? ::: ## The Goemans–Williamson SDP relaxation {.smaller} ::: {.box-yellow style="text-align: center; font-size: 1.25em;"} **Exercise:** Lift and relax $\min\big(x^\top Ax:x_i^2=1\big) \quad (\dagger)$. ::: . . . **Lifting:** $(\dagger)$ is a purely quadratic problem in $x$ (i.e. only quadratic terms in $x$ in both the objective function and the constraints). One can **lift** this type of problem to a matrix optimization problem: $$\min\big(x^\top Ax:x_i^2=1\big) = \min\big(\inr{A, Z}:Z\succeq 0, {\rm rank}(Z) = 1, Z_{ii}=1\big).$$ **SDP relaxation:** drop the rank constraint to get the SDP problem: $$\min\big(\inr{A,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{ii}=1\big). \quad (\dagger\dagger)$$ :::{.box-red} $(\dagger\dagger)$ is the Goemans–Williamson SDP relaxation of the Max-Cut problem. ::: . . . ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: :::{.box-blue} Usually $(\dagger\dagger)$ does not have a rank one solution and so $(\dagger)$ and $(\dagger\dagger)$ are not equivalent (in general). **Question:** How can we find a solution to the Max-Cut problem from a solution to $(\dagger\dagger)$? **Solution:** [**Rounding:**]{.blue} from $Z^*$ a solution to $(\dagger\dagger)$, we draw $G\sim\cN(0, Z^*)$ and set $x^{**} = {\rm sign}(G)$. ::: ## The Goemans–Williamson Theorem {.smaller} ::: {.box-red} Let $Z^*$ be a solution to, $$\min\big(\inr{A,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{ii}=1\big). \quad (\dagger\dagger)$$ Let $G\sim\cN(0, Z^*)$ and set $x^{**} = {\rm sign}(G)$. Then, $$\E\Big[\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}(1- x^{**}_i x^{**}_j)\Big]\geq \alpha_{GW}\cdot{\rm OPT}$$ where $\alpha_{GW} = \frac{2}{\pi}\min_{0\leq \theta\leq \pi}\frac{\theta}{1-\cos(\theta)} \approx 0.878$ and ${\rm OPT}$ is the value of the optimal solution to the Max-Cut problem. ::: . . . :::{.box-yellow} **Question:** Tell what is random in the result above. ::: ::: {.box-blue} **Idea:** Goemans-Williamson approximating solution to the Max-Cut problem is a *polynomial time randomized algorithm*. There are many such algorithms in computer science. The class of such algorithms with polynomial time complexity is called BPP (Bounded-error Probabilistic Polynomial time). It is believed that BPP = P. ::: ## Sketch of Proof of the Goemans-Williamson Theorem {style="font-size: 0.9em;"} The proof relies on evaluating the expected contribution of a single pair $(i,j)$ and comparing it to the SDP's contribution. ::: {.fragment .mt-4} **1. The Bivariate Gaussian** Since $G \sim \cN(0, Z^*)$, the marginals $G_i$ and $G_j$ form a zero-mean bivariate normal distribution. Their variances are $Z^*_{ii}=1$ and $Z^*_{jj}=1$, and their covariance is $Z^*_{ij}$. ::: ::: {.fragment .mt-4} **2. Sheppard's Lemma (Geometric Probability)** The probability that $G_i$ and $G_j$ have *different* signs is determined by the angle between them. By setting $Z^*_{ij} = \cos(\theta)$, the probability they are separated by the random hyperplane (i.e., $x^{**}_i \neq x^{**}_j$) is exactly $\frac{\theta}{\pi}$. ::: ::: {.fragment .mt-4} **3. Term-by-Term Ratio** We compare the expected cut for the pair $(i,j)$ against the SDP's relaxed value for that same pair: $$ \frac{\text{Expected Cut}_{ij}}{\text{SDP Value}_{ij}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{\theta}{\pi}}{\frac{1}{4}(1 - Z^*_{ij})} = \frac{2}{\pi} \frac{\theta}{1 - \cos(\theta)} $$ ::: ::: {.fragment .mt-4} **4. Global Bound** Because this ratio is bounded below by $\alpha_{GW} \approx 0.878$ for *every* angle $\theta \in [0, \pi]$, we sum over all pairs $(i,j)$ by linearity of expectation to get: $$ \E[\text{Cut}] \geq \alpha_{GW} \cdot \text{SDP-VAL} \geq \alpha_{GW} \cdot \text{OPT} $$ ::: ## Can we do better than the $\alpha_{GW}$ factor? :::{.box-yellow} **Question:** Is it possible to construct in polynomial time an approximating solution to the Max-Cut problem that can do better than the $\alpha_{GW}$ factor? That is to construct (in polynomial time) a cut $x^\circ$ such that $$\frac14\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}(1- x^{\circ}_i x^{\circ}_j) > \alpha_{GW}\cdot{\rm OPT} ?$$ (in a deterministic or randomized way). ::: . . . ::: {style="height: 50px;"} ::: :::{.box-red} **OpenAI (6/10/26) answer:** No, it is not possible to construct in polynomial time an approximating solution to the Max-Cut problem that can do better than the $\alpha_{GW}$ factor (unless $P=NP$) for both deterministic and randomized algorithms. ::: ## Lifting linear and quadratic constraints {.smaller} The constraint $\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0$ is **linear** in $x$, hence not a linear function of $xx^\top$. One can still lift it by adding one coordinate: $$\begin{pmatrix}1\\x\end{pmatrix}\rightsquigarrow Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\\x&xx^\top\end{pmatrix}.$$ The equal-size community problem becomes the SDP $$\min\big(\inr{L,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{00}=1,\,Z_{ii}=1,\,\inr{Z,A}=0\big),$$ after dropping the rank. Linear terms live in the first row and column of $Z$. . . . ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: one extra dimension" icon=false} Quadratic terms live in $xx^\top$. Linear terms appear as soon as one lifts $(1,x)$ instead of $x$. ::: # Introduction ## The community detection problem (1/2) - [Nodes]{.blue} are people; an [edge]{.blue} is a connection (messages, friendship, collaboration). - **Goal:** find groups of nodes that are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the graph. - These groups may be groups of friends, or people who share interests. - Once the communities are found, we may: 1. Look for **influencers** and send them advertisements, or approach them directly. 2. Understand the **common features** of the nodes inside this community to understand how the community was created and what share the people inside of it. ## The community detection problem (2/2) ![](images/community_detection.png){width=46% fig-align="center" fig-alt="Community detection network diagram"} ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: density, not just connectivity" icon=false style="font-size: 0.85em;"} A community is not a connected component. It is a set of nodes with a **higher density of internal edges** than of edges leaving the set. ::: ## Connectivity and connected components {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (connected graph)" icon=false} $G=(V,E)$ is **connected** if a path of edges links all the nodes. A **connected component** is a connected subgraph with no edge to its complement. A **connected partition** is a partition of $V$ into connected components. ::: - Weighted version: the edges of the path must have **nonzero weight**. Unweighted graphs correspond to $W=(1)_{i,j}$. ::: {.callout-caution title="Remark for community detection" icon=false} A nontrivial connected partition is an **ideal** setting: the communities do not interact. Rare in practice, but a good guide for algorithms. ::: # The Laplacian of a graph ## Definition of the Laplacian {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (Laplacian)" icon=false} Let $A$ be the adjacency matrix of $G$. The **Laplacian** is $$L=D-A,\qquad D={\rm diag}(d),\qquad d_i=\sum_{j\in V}A_{ij}$$ where $d_i$ is the **degree** of node $i$. ::: - Other definitions exist; we use this one throughout. - If $G$ is undirected, then $L$ is **symmetric**: the spectral theorem applies, and $L=PDP^\top$ with $P$ orthogonal. - The **spectrum** of $L$ is the key object of spectral community detection. ## Quadratic form and first properties {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} Let $G=(V,E,W)$ be undirected with $W_{ij}\geq 0$. Then: 1. $f^\top Lf=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in E}W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2$ for every $f\in\R^{|V|}$; 2. $L$ is symmetric **positive semidefinite**; 3. $0$ is an eigenvalue and $L\mathbf{1}=0$. ::: **Proof.** . . . 1. $f^\top(D-A)f=\sum_i d_if_i^2-\sum_{(i,j)\in E}f_iW_{ij}f_j=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in E}W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2$. 2. The right-hand side is $\geq 0$, so $L\succeq 0$. 3. $(L\mathbf{1})_i=d_i-\sum_j A_{ij}=0$. $\square$ ## Multiplicity of $0$ and connected components {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} For an undirected weighted graph with nonnegative weights, the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $0$ of $L$ equals the **number of connected components**. Moreover ${\rm Ker}(L)$ is spanned by $\mathbf{1}_{V_1},\ldots,\mathbf{1}_{V_k}$, where $V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k$ is the partition of $V$ into connected components. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: the kernel of $L$ sees the communities" icon=false} In the ideal case, the indicators of the communities are eigenvectors for $\lambda=0$. Spectral methods start from this fact. ::: ## Proof sketch: one connected component Assume $G$ is connected and $Lf=0$. Then $f^\top Lf=0$, so $$\sum_{(i,j)\in E}W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2=0.$$ . . . - Weights are nonnegative, so $W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2=0$ on every edge: $W_{ij}=0$ or $f_i=f_j$. - Connectivity: any $i,j$ are joined by a path of **positive** weights, so $f$ is constant along the path. - Hence $f$ is constant: ${\rm Ker}(L)={\rm span}(\mathbf{1})$. ## Proof sketch: several components {.smaller} Up to reordering the nodes, $$L=\begin{pmatrix}L_1&&\\&\ddots&\\&&L_k\end{pmatrix},$$ where $L_i$ is the Laplacian of the $i$-th connected component. . . . - Each $L_i$ has kernel spanned by the constant vector on $V_i$, so $\mathbf{1}_{V_i}\in{\rm Ker}(L)$. - Conversely $Lf=0$ if and only if $L_if=0$ on each block, so $f$ is constant on each $V_i$. - Therefore ${\rm Ker}(L)={\rm span}(\mathbf{1}_{V_1},\ldots,\mathbf{1}_{V_k})$. ::: {.callout-caution title="Remark" icon=false} The same statement holds for unweighted undirected graphs, by taking $W=(1)_{i,j}$. ::: ## Example: the complete graph $K_n$ The Laplacian of $K_n$ is $$L=nI_n-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top=\begin{pmatrix}n-1&-1&\cdots&-1\\-1&n-1&\cdots&-1\\\vdots&&\ddots&\vdots\\-1&-1&\cdots&n-1\end{pmatrix}.$$ - If $Lf=0$, then $nf=\inr{f,\mathbf{1}}\mathbf{1}$, so $f\in{\rm span}(\mathbf{1})$. - The multiplicity of $0$ is $1$, as expected: $K_n$ is connected. ## Why is $L$ called a Laplacian? Newton's law of cooling {.smaller} :::: {.columns style="display: flex; align-items: center;"} ::: {.column width="62%"} Imagine temperatures $T_i$ on the nodes. Heat flows **in proportion to the temperature difference**: $$\frac{dT_i}{dt}=-\kappa\sum_{j\in V}A_{ij}(T_i-T_j).$$ - Node $i$ exchanges heat only with its neighbours. - In vector form: $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-\kappa(D-A)T=-\kappa LT$. - Compare with the heat equation $\partial_t u=\alpha\Delta u$: one identifies $L$ with $-\Delta$. ::: ::: {.column width="38%"} ![](images/Newton_heat_flow.jpeg){width=70% fig-align="center" fig-alt="Newton heat flow"} ::: :::: ::: {style="height: 80px;"} ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: a discrete Laplacian" icon=false} The graph Laplacian is the *discrete analog* of the Laplacian of the heat equation. ::: # Principle of spectral methods ## Ideal setting: disjoint communities - **Ideal case:** the communities are the connected components. They do not interact. - Almost never true in practice (a few inter-community edges always exist), but a good guide. - Then ${\rm Ker}(L)={\rm span}(\mathbf{1}_{V_1},\ldots,\mathbf{1}_{V_k})$. - The indicators $\mathbf{1}_{V_i}$ are hard to read off $L$. An **orthonormal basis** $u_1,\ldots,u_k$ of ${\rm Ker}(L)$ is easy. ## The spectral method in two steps 1. Cluster the $|V|$ **row vectors** $y_i\in\R^k$ of the matrix $[u_1|\cdots|u_k]$ into $k$ clusters $C_1,\ldots,C_k$. 2. Return $V_p=\{i\in V:y_i\in C_p\}$. These are the detected communities. . . . ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: cluster the rows, not the nodes" icon=false} Each node $i$ is represented by the $i$-th row of the eigenbasis matrix. Clustering these rows clusters the nodes. ::: ## Why the rotation does not destroy the clusters {.smaller} - $\{\mathbf{1}_{V_p}/\sqrt{|V_p|}\}_p$ is an orthonormal basis of ${\rm Ker}(L)$. - So is $\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}$: there is $R\in{\rm O}(k)$ with $$[u_1|\cdots|u_k]=\big[\mathbf{1}_{V_1}/\sqrt{|V_1|}|\cdots|\mathbf{1}_{V_k}/\sqrt{|V_k|}\big]R.$$ - The rows of the indicator matrix take only $k$ distinct values. A $k$-means on these rows recovers the components **exactly**. - A rotation of $\R^k$ preserves this clustering. . . . **In practice** $G$ is not a disjoint union: look at the eigenspace of the **$k$ smallest eigenvalues**, not only the kernel. Choose $k$ by an elbow in the spectrum, or by a modularity function. ## Graph cuts and modularity {.smaller} Detecting communities $\iff$ finding a partition that **minimizes the inter-community weight** while keeping the communities **large enough**. - A **cut** is a partition of $V$. - A **modularity** quantifies intra- versus inter-community mass. For $A,B\subset V$, $$W(A,B)=\sum_{\substack{(i,j)\in E\\(i,j)\in A\times B}}(W_{ij}+W_{ji})=2\sum_{\substack{(i,j)\in E\\(i,j)\in A\times B}}W_{ij}.$$ The **cut** of a partition $V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k$ is $${\rm cut}(V_1,\ldots,V_k)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^k W(V_i,V_i^c).$$ ## The mincut problem {.smaller} For two communities, encode $V_1$ by $x\in\{0,1\}^{|V|}$: $${\rm cut}(V_1,V_1^c)=2\sum_{(i,j)\in E}x_i W_{ij}(1-x_j).$$ $$\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{|V|}}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}x_i W_{ij}(1-x_j).$$ - Solvable by the **Stoer–Wagner** algorithm. - In practice it often returns a singleton: the node of **smallest degree**. . . . ::: {.callout-caution title="Remark" icon=false} A singleton is not a community. One must force the parts to have sufficient size. ::: ## RatioCut ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (RatioCut)" icon=false} $${\rm RatioCut}(V_1,\ldots,V_k)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{W(V_i,V_i^c)}{|V_i|}.$$ ::: - The factor $1/|V_i|$ penalizes small communities. - Minimizing RatioCut over $\cP_k(V)$ is **NP-hard** in general. - We rewrite it as a vector (then matrix) problem and **convexify the constraint**. The relaxation is the spectral method. ## Membership vector for two communities {.smaller} For $V_1\subset V$, set $$f_i^{V_1}=\begin{cases}\sqrt{|V_1^c|/|V_1|}& \text{if }i\in V_1,\\[4pt]-\sqrt{|V_1|/|V_1^c|}& \text{if }i\notin V_1.\end{cases}$$ ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} Let $L$ be the Laplacian of an undirected weighted graph, and $n=|V|$. Then 1. $\inr{f^{V_1},\mathbf{1}}=0$ and $\norm{f^{V_1}}_2^2=n$; 2. $(f^{V_1})^\top L f^{V_1}=n\,{\rm RatioCut}(V_1,V_1^c)$. ::: - So minimizing RatioCut $\iff$ minimizing $f^\top Lf$ over these discrete vectors $f^{V_1}$. ## Proof sketch of the RatioCut identity {.smaller} From the quadratic form, $$(f^{V_1})^\top Lf^{V_1}=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in E}W_{ij}(f_i^{V_1}-f_j^{V_1})^2.$$ - The difference $f_i^{V_1}-f_j^{V_1}$ is nonzero only across the cut. - On a cut edge, $$\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{|V_1^c|}{|V_1|}}+\sqrt{\tfrac{|V_1|}{|V_1^c|}}\Big)^2=\frac{n}{|V_1|}+\frac{n}{|V_1^c|}.$$ - Summing both orientations of the cut gives $n\,{\rm RatioCut}(V_1,V_1^c)$. - The two constraints: $\norm{f^{V_1}}_2^2=|V_1|+|V_1^c|=n$ and $\inr{f^{V_1},\mathbf{1}}=0$. $\square$ ## Convex relaxation for $k=2$ {.smaller} Three equivalent **discrete** problems: $$\min_{V_1\subset V}(f^{V_1})^\top Lf^{V_1},\qquad\min_{V_1\subset V}\big((f^{V_1})^\top Lf^{V_1}:\norm{f^{V_1}}_2^2=n,\,\inr{f^{V_1},\mathbf{1}}=0\big),$$ and $\min_{V_1}{\rm RatioCut}(V_1,V_1^c)$. All are NP-hard. - The map $f\mapsto f^\top Lf$ is **convex** (${\rm Hess}=2L\succeq 0$). - The difficulty is the discrete constraint $f=f^{V_1}$. - **Relax** it to $f\in\R^{|V|}$: $$\min_{f\in\R^{|V|}}\big(f^\top Lf:\norm{f}_2^2=1,\,\inr{f,\mathbf{1}}=0\big).$$ ## The Fiedler vector {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (Fiedler vector)" icon=false} A **Fiedler vector** of $L$ is an eigenvector for the **second smallest** eigenvalue. That eigenvalue is the **algebraic connectivity**. ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} The Fiedler vectors are exactly the solutions of the relaxed problem. ::: **Proof.** Write $0=\lambda_1\leq\lambda_2\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n$ and $u_1=\mathbf{1}$. If $\norm{f}_2=1$ and $\inr{f,\mathbf{1}}=0$, $$f^\top Lf=\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i\inr{u_i,f}^2\geq\lambda_2,$$ with equality at $f=u_2$. $\square$ ## From a Fiedler vector to two communities - A Fiedler vector $u_2$ approximates the two-valued membership vector $f^{V_1^*}$. - Its coordinates should concentrate around **two values**. - Cluster the coordinates of $u_2$ into two classes $C_1,C_2$ on $\R$. - The communities are $\{i:u_{2i}\in C_1\}$ and $\{i:u_{2i}\in C_2\}$. . . . This **is** the spectral method for $k=2$, with first eigenvector $u_1=\mathbf{1}$ (clustering the rows of $[u_1|u_2]$ is the same as clustering the coordinates of $u_2$). ## Membership matrix for $k$ communities {.smaller} To a partition $V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k$ associate $H\in\R^{|V|\times k}$ with columns $h_j=\mathbf{1}_{V_j}/\sqrt{|V_j|}$: $$H_{ij}=\begin{cases}1/\sqrt{|V_j|}& \text{if }i\in V_j,\\0& \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$ ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} $H^\top H=I_k$ and ${\rm RatioCut}(V_1,\ldots,V_k)={\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)$. ::: - $H^\top H=I_k$: the $V_j$ are disjoint, and $\sum_{i\in V_j}1/|V_j|=1$. - ${\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)=\sum_p h_p^\top Lh_p=\sum_p W(V_p,V_p^c)/(2|V_p|)$. ## Relaxation for $k$ communities {.smaller} The discrete problems $\min{\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)$ over membership matrices $H$ are NP-hard. The objective $H\mapsto{\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)$ is convex. Relax the combinatorial constraint: $$\min_{\substack{H\in\R^{|V|\times k}\\H^\top H=I_k}}{\rm Tr}(H^\top LH).$$ Write $L=UDU^\top$ with $0=\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n$. Then $${\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)=\sum_i\lambda_i\norm{a_i}_2^2,\qquad\sum_i\norm{a_i}_2^2=k,$$ where $a_i$ is the $i$-th row of $U^\top H$. The minimum is $\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i$, attained when $${\rm span}(h_1,\ldots,h_k)={\rm span}(u_1,\ldots,u_k).$$ - The solutions are orthonormal bases of the eigenspace of the **$k$ smallest eigenvalues**. - Cluster the $n$ rows of $H$ into $k$ groups: this is again the spectral method. ## Algorithm of the spectral method {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Algorithm (spectral method)" icon=false} **Input:** Laplacian $L$ of $G$, and $k$. 1. Compute an orthonormal basis of $k$ eigenvectors for the $k$ smallest eigenvalues of $L$. 2. Form the $n\times k$ matrix $H$ with these columns. 3. Cluster the $n$ rows $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\R^k$ into $k$ clusters $C_1,\ldots,C_k$. 4. **Output:** communities $\{i:y_i\in C_p\}$, $p=1,\ldots,k$. ::: - Justified by the RatioCut relaxation, or by the ideal connected-component picture. - Choose $k$ by an **elbow** in the spectrum of $L$, or by evaluating a modularity (e.g. RatioCut) as a function of $k$. # Probabilistic graph models ## Why a random graph? - Until now every edge was observed. - In applications (genes, companies, \ldots) some links are **missing** or **uncertain**. - One then assumes a **probabilistic model** under the observations, and still wants the communities. - The same spectral method will be applied to the Laplacian of the **observed** adjacency matrix. ## The Erdős–Rényi model ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (Erdős–Rényi)" icon=false} $G\sim G(n,p)$ is an undirected unweighted graph on $n$ nodes with $$A_{ij}=A_{ji},\qquad A_{ii}=1,\qquad (A_{ij})_{j>i}\ \text{i.i.d. }{\rm Bern}(p).$$ ::: - Every pair of distinct nodes is connected independently with probability $p$. - No community structure: a **null model**. ## The stochastic block model ::: {.callout-note title="Definition (SBM)" icon=false} $G\sim G(n,p,q)$ with $0\leq qq$). - **Problem:** given one draw of $G$, recover $V_1$ and $V_1^c$. ## Likelihood in the two-community SBM {.smaller} Given $A$, the likelihood at $(V_1,p,q)$ is $$\cL(V_1,p,q)=\prod_{(i,j)\in\cC}p^{A_{ij}}(1-p)^{1-A_{ij}}\prod_{(i,j)\in\cC^c}q^{A_{ij}}(1-q)^{1-A_{ij}},$$ where $\cC$ is the set of intra-community pairs $iP_{\cC^c}$, then $\hat p=P_{\cC}$, $\hat q=P_{\cC^c}$; - otherwise $\hat p=\hat q=(P_{\cC}+P_{\cC^c})/2$, and the value does **not** depend on $V_1$. The remaining problem in $V_1$ is to maximize an entropy under $P_{\cC}\geq P_{\cC^c}$. Since $P_{\cC}+P_{\cC^c}$ is constant, this is equivalent to **minimizing** $P_{\cC^c}$. . . . $$P_{\cC^c}={\rm RatioCut}(V_1,V_1^c).$$ ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: MLE is RatioCut" icon=false} For two equal-size communities, the MLE in the SBM is the RatioCut problem. ::: ## An equivalent discrete program {.smaller} ::: {.callout-caution title="Remark" icon=false} For $|V_1|=n/2$ one has $f^{V_1}\in\{-1,1\}^n$, so the MLE / RatioCut problem is $$\min\big(x^\top Lx:\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0,\,x\in\{-1,1\}^n\big).$$ Since $x^\top Lx=-x^\top Ax+\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}$ and the second term is constant, this is also $$\max\big(x^\top Ax:\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0,\,x\in\{-1,1\}^n\big).$$ ::: This last form is the one we shall lift to an SDP. ## Detectability: isolated nodes {.smaller} If a node of $V_1$ has **no edge** inside $V_1$, there is no reason to assign it to $V_1$. Exact recovery then fails. ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} If $p\leq\log(n/2)\,/\,(n/2-2)$, then $\PP[\text{some node of }V_1\text{ is isolated in }V_1]\geq 1/2$. ::: **Proof idea.** Let $A_i$ be the event that $i\in V_1$ is isolated in $V_1$, and $N=|V_1|-1$. Then $\PP[A_i]=(1-p)^N$. A Bonferroni bound $$\PP[\cup_i A_i]\geq(N+1)(1-p)^N-(N+1)N(1-p)^{2N-1}$$ is at least $1/2$ as soon as $p\leq(\log N)/(N-1)$. $\square$ - Exact recovery therefore requires $p\gtrsim\alpha\log n\,/\,n$. The hard regime is $q=\beta\log n\,/\,n$ with $\beta<\alpha$. ## Information-theoretic phase transition {.smaller} ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem (phase transition in the equal-size SBM)" icon=false} Let $\hat V_1$ be the MLE (minimal RatioCut). If $p=\alpha\log n\,/\,n$ and $q=\beta\log n\,/\,n$, then: - if $\sqrt{\alpha}-\sqrt{\beta}>\sqrt{2}$, then $\hat V_1,\hat V_1^c$ recover $V_1,V_1^c$ with high probability; - if $\sqrt{\alpha}-\sqrt{\beta}<\sqrt{2}$, **no** algorithm succeeds with probability $\geq 1/2$. ::: - A sharp threshold, but the MLE is not computable. - The practical question: can a **spectral** or **SDP** method attain (or approach) this threshold? ## Spectral method for the equal-size SBM {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Lemma" icon=false} If $|V_1|=|V_1^c|=n/2$, the following are equivalent: 1. $u_2$ is a Fiedler vector of $\E L=\E(D-A)$; 2. $u_2$ is a leading eigenvector of $$\E A-\Big[n\tfrac{p+q}{2}+(1-p)\Big]\Big(\tfrac{\mathbf{1}}{\sqrt n}\Big)\Big(\tfrac{\mathbf{1}}{\sqrt n}\Big)^\top.$$ ::: **Why.** All mean degrees are equal, so $\E D$ is a multiple of $I_n$. Eigenvectors of $\E L$ and $\E A$ coincide (eigenvalues reversed). The leading eigenspace of $\E A$ is ${\rm span}(\mathbf{1})$; removing it leaves the Fiedler direction. ## A practical spectral problem We do not know $\E A$, $p$ or $q$. Estimate: - $\E A$ by $A$; - $(p+q)/2$ by the edge density $$\lambda=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i0$ from the rest of the spectrum, then $$\min_{\alpha\in\{\pm 1\}}\norm{u_i(A)-\alpha u_i(B)}_2\leq 2^{3/2}\frac{\norm{A-B}_2}{\delta}.$$ ::: Apply it to $A=\bar x\bar x^\top$ (gap $\delta=n$) and $B=\hat Z$. ## Outline of the proof Write $\cM_{\rm opt}=\{Z:Z\succeq 0,\,{\rm diag}(Z)\preceq I_n\}$. Three steps: 1. **Oracle:** $\bar Z=\bar x\bar x^\top$ maximizes $Z\mapsto\inr{\E(A-\lambda J_n),Z}$ over $\cM_{\rm opt}$ (as in the oracle proposition). 2. **Uniform concentration:** with high probability, $$\sup_{Z\in\cM_{\rm opt}}\big|\inr{(A-\lambda J_n)-\E(A-\lambda J_n),Z}\big|$$ is small. This is the **probabilistic** step. 3. **Curvature** at the optimum: $\inr{\E(A-\lambda J_n),\bar Z-Z}\gtrsim\norm{Z-\bar Z}_1$. ## Grothendieck's inequality {.smaller} ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem (Grothendieck)" icon=false} If $\big|\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}s_it_j\big|\leq 1$ for all $s_i,t_j\in\{\pm 1\}$, then for every Hilbert space $H$ and unit vectors $u_i,v_j$, $\big|\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}\inr{u_i,v_j}\big|\leq K_G$, with $K_G\leq 1.783$. ::: Write $\cM_1=\{st^\top:s,t\in\{\pm 1\}^n\}$ and $\cM_G=\{XY^\top:\text{rows of }X,Y\text{ in }B_2^n\}$. ::: {.callout-note title="Corollary" icon=false} $\displaystyle\sup_{Z\in\cM_G}\inr{B,Z}\leq K_G\sup_{Z\in\cM_1}\inr{B,Z}=K_G\norm{B}_{\infty\to 1}$. ::: ## Why Grothendieck applies here {.smaller} ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} $\cM_{\rm opt}\subset\cM_G$. ::: If $Z\succeq 0$ then $Z=XX^\top$, and ${\rm diag}(Z)\preceq I_n$ means $\norm{X_{i\bullet}}_2\leq 1$. . . . Therefore $$\sup_{Z\in\cM_{\rm opt}}\big|\inr{(A-\lambda J_n)-\E(\cdots),Z}\big|\leq K_G\norm{A-\E A}_{\infty\to 1}+K_G|\lambda-\E\lambda|\,\norm{J_n}_{\infty\to 1}.$$ - Bound $\norm{A-\E A}_{\infty\to 1}$ and $|\lambda-\E\lambda|$ by **Bernstein** and a union bound. - If $\bar p=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i9/n$, then with probability $1-e^3 5^{-n}$, $$\norm{A-\E A}_{\infty\to 1}\leq 6n(n-1)\sqrt{\bar p/n}.$$ # Exact recovery by a dual certificate ## Weak duality for SDP problems {.smaller} A standard SDP and its dual: $$\min\big(\inr{C,X}:X\succeq 0,\,\cA(X)=b\big),\qquad\max\big(\inr{\lambda,b}:C-\cA^\top(\lambda)\succeq 0\big).$$ - **Weak duality:** $\inr{C,X}\geq\inr{\lambda,b}$ for every feasible pair. - If a feasible pair saturates the inequality, both are optimal: this is a **dual certificate**. ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem (strong duality for SDP)" icon=false} If there exist $X_0\succ 0$ with $\cA(X_0)=b$ and $\lambda_0$ with $C-\cA^\top(\lambda_0)\succ 0$ (Slater), then both problems attain their optima and there is no duality gap. ::: ## The dual-certificate method ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} If $X^*$ is primal-feasible, $\lambda^*$ is dual-feasible, and $\inr{C,X^*}=\inr{b,\lambda^*}$, then both are optimal. ::: **Strategy.** 1. Start from an NP-hard problem $(P_0)$ (here, recover $g=f^{V_1}$). 2. Convexify it into an SDP $(P)$. 3. Take the candidate $X_0=gg^\top$ and **build** a dual-feasible $\lambda_0$ with equal objective values. 4. Then $X_0$ solves $(P)$: one has solved $(P_0)$ by solving $(P)$. ## Another SDP, designed for exact recovery {.smaller} The theoretical problem with $\E L$ has unique solutions $f^{V_1}$ and $f^{V_1^c}$. We observe only $L$, so we solve the empirical version $$\max\big(x^\top Ax:\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0,\,x\in\{-1,1\}^n\big).$$ - Dropping $\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0$ makes $\mathbf{1}$ optimal: the trivial cut. - Penalize: replace the objective by $x^\top Ax-\lambda\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}^2$, and add the constant $\lambda\norm{x}_2^2$. - For $\lambda=1/2$ this is $x^\top Bx$ with $$B=2A-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top-I_n,\qquad B_{ij}=\begin{cases}0&i=j,\\1&(i,j)\in E,\\-1&(i,j)\notin E.\end{cases}$$ ## Lifted SDP $$\max\big(x^\top Bx:x\in\{-1,1\}^n\big)\quad\rightsquigarrow\quad\max\big(\inr{B,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{ii}=1\big).$$ - The rank constraint has been dropped: this is an SDP. - From a solution $\hat Z$: take a leading eigenvector and its sign, or **round** $G\sim\cN(0,\hat Z)$ and take ${\rm sign}(G)$. - **Goal:** prove that $gg^\top$ is the **unique** solution, by a **strict** dual certificate. ## Dual of the community-detection SDP {.smaller} The dual can be written $$\min\big({\rm Tr}(Y):Y-B\succeq 0,\,Y\text{ diagonal}\big).$$ Weak duality: for primal-feasible $Z$ and dual-feasible $Y$, $$\inr{B,Z}\leq{\rm Tr}(Y).$$ $Y$ **certifies** a feasible $Z$ when $\inr{B,Z}={\rm Tr}(Y)$, i.e. $\inr{B-Y,Z}=0$. . . . For uniqueness one needs a **strict** certificate: ${\rm Ker}(B-Y)$ of dimension $1$. ::: {.callout-note title="Lemma" icon=false} If $Y$ certifies $gg^\top$ and $\dim{\rm Ker}(B-Y)=1$, then $gg^\top$ is the unique primal solution. ::: ## Construction of the certificate Conditions on $Y$: diagonal, $Y\succeq B$, $(B-Y)g=0$, and $\lambda_2(Y-B)>0$. The first three force $$Y_{ii}=\frac{(Bg)_i}{g_i}=\frac{2(Ag)_i}{g_i}-1,\qquad Y_{ij}=0\text{ for }i\neq j.$$ ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} If $\lambda_2(Y-B)>0$, then $gg^\top$ is the unique solution of the SDP. ::: It remains to prove $\lambda_2(Y-B)>0$ **with high probability** in the SBM. ## Deterministic plus concentration Write $\square=(\alpha-\beta)\log n$ when $p=\alpha\log n\,/\,n$ and $q=\beta\log n\,/\,n$. Enough to show: 1. $\lambda_2(\E(Y-B))=\square$; 2. $\norm{(Y-B)-\E(Y-B)}_{\rm op}<\square$ with high probability. Weyl / Courant–Fischer then gives $$\lambda_2(Y-B)\geq\lambda_2(\E(Y-B))-\norm{(Y-B)-\E(Y-B)}_{\rm op}>0.$$ ## Spectrum of the mean certificate {.smaller} A computation with $g\in\{\pm 1\}^n$ and $\inr{g,\mathbf{1}}=0$ yields $$\E(Y-B)=n(p-q)I_n-(p-q)gg^\top+(1-p-q)\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top.$$ - $g$ is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $0$. - On $g^\perp$, if $p+q\leq 1$ then $v^\top\E(Y-B)v\geq n(p-q)$, with equality for $v\perp\mathbf{1}$. - Hence $\lambda_2(\E(Y-B))=n(p-q)=(\alpha-\beta)\log n$. ## Decomposing intra- and inter-community edges ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Adjacency matrix $A=A^{\sim}+A^{\not\sim}$: intra-community blocks (blue) and inter-community blocks (red).](matrix_lifting_SDP_relaxation_files/figure-revealjs/fig-decomp-A-1.svg){#fig-decomp-A fig-align='center' width=78%} ::: ::: - $Y-B=2\big[(D^{\sim}-A^{\sim})-(D^{\not\sim}-A^{\not\sim})\big]+\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$: difference of the two Laplacians. - Each Laplacian is a sum of independent matrices $\Delta_{ij}=E_{ii}+E_{jj}-E_{ij}-E_{ji}$. ## Matrix Bernstein ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem (matrix Bernstein)" icon=false} Let $X_k$ be independent centered symmetric $d\times d$ matrices with $\lambda_{\max}(X_k)\leq R$ a.s. Then, with probability at least $1-d\exp(-t)$, $$\lambda_{\max}\Big(\frac1n\sum_k X_k\Big)\leq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2t}{n}}+\frac{2Rt}{3n},\qquad\sigma^2=\Big\|\frac1n\sum_k\E X_k^2\Big\|_{\rm op}.$$ ::: - The dimension $d$ appears in the probability. Here $t\sim\log n$, so it only costs constants. - Applied to the sum over intra- and inter-edges: $R=2$ and $\sigma^2\leq n(p+q)$. ## Exact recovery by SDP {.smaller} ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem" icon=false} Let $p=\alpha\log n\,/\,n$, $q=\beta\log n\,/\,n$ with $0<\beta<\alpha$ and $p+q<1$, and $|V_1|=n/2$. Then $$\{gg^\top\}=\argmax\big(\inr{B,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{ii}=1\big)$$ with probability at least $1-2/n^\eps$, as soon as $$\sqrt{2(1+\eps)(\alpha+\beta)}+\frac{4(1+\eps)}{3}<\alpha-\beta.$$ ::: - An NP-hard problem is solved, for most SBM graphs, by an SDP. - The threshold is more restrictive than $\sqrt{\alpha}-\sqrt{\beta}>\sqrt{2}$. ## No computational gap {.smaller} ::: {.callout-important title="Theorem (improved analysis)" icon=false} Under the same SBM assumptions, $gg^\top$ is the unique SDP solution with high probability as soon as $$\sqrt{\alpha}-\sqrt{\beta}>\sqrt{2}.$$ ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} - The SDP attains the **information-theoretic** threshold. - There is **no computational gap** for two equal-size communities in the SBM. ::: ::: {.column width="52%"} ::: {.callout-tip title="Idea: randomness does things well" icon=false} NP-hard problems can become easy under a natural random model. Convex relaxation — of the objective, of the constraint, or by matrix lifting — is the right device. ::: ::: :::: ## Dual certificate for basis pursuit {.smaller} The same idea applies to $$\min\big(\norm{t}_1:At=y\big).$$ - Subdifferential: $0\in\partial^-\norm{\cdot}_1(x^*)+\mathrm{Im}(A^\top)$ iff there is $\beta^*$ with $$\norm{A^\top\beta^*}_\infty\leq 1,\qquad (A^\top\beta^*)_I={\rm sgn}(x^*_I),\quad I={\rm supp}(x^*).$$ - Lagrangian dual: $\max\big(\inr{\beta,y}:\norm{A^\top\beta}_\infty\leq 1\big)$. - Weak duality: $\norm{t}_1\geq\inr{\beta,y}$. Equality plus dual feasibility certifies $t^*$. A **strict** certificate rules out every other feasible $t$: that is uniqueness. ::: {.callout-note title="Proposition" icon=false} Under strong duality, if $\lambda^*$ solves the dual then $x^*$ solves the primal if and only if $\varphi(x^*)=\psi(\lambda^*)$. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
